video.title: Data structures: Choose by the job
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — the students’ programming lecturer (main character)
Mr Okafor — the students’ data science lecturer (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: A student’s attendance app checked each name against a list of twenty thousand students. Every check walked the whole list, and the app crawled. He changed one line, from a list to a set, and it became instant.
Today: data structures, and how to choose one by the job.

Choose a structure by what the job does most. A list keeps items in order, by position. A stack takes from the top; a queue from the front. A set answers one question fast: is it there? And a dictionary finds a value by its key.

A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates. Push adds to the top, and pop takes from the top. The back button, undo and the call stack all work this way. In Python, a list’s append and pop make a stack.

A queue is first in, first out, like the canteen line or the printer. Items join at the back and leave from the front. Taking from the front of a big list is slow, because every item shifts along. For big queues, Python has a deque.

Here’s a classic job for a stack: checking brackets. Each opening bracket is pushed. Each closing one pops the top, which must be its partner. If every pair matches and the stack ends empty, the brackets balance.
Quick check! Your notes app keeps an undo history: the last change made is the first one undone. Which structure fits?
A stack: last in, first out. Each change is pushed, and undo pops the newest. A queue would undo your oldest change first, which nobody wants.

Sets and dictionaries jump straight to where an item would be, using a hash. So checking whether x is in a set takes about one step, however big it grows. A list checks its items one by one. The price: a set keeps no order and no repeats.

A dictionary finds a value by its key. To count votes, use each candidate as a key, and add one each time it appears. Get, with a default of zero, handles a candidate seen for the first time. One pass, and every count is ready.
In the app, open Stacks and queues. Push and pop the undo stack of a notes app, then serve a queue at the bank. Before each step, predict what comes out next.
Your turn. Your program checks, thousands of times, whether a student ID is registered. Which structure should hold the registered IDs?

A set: about one step per check. In short: choose a structure by the operations the job needs. Stacks are last in, first out; queues first in, first out. Sets answer is it there, and dictionaries find values by key.

Try it yourself: write the bracket checker in full. Push each opening bracket, and on each closing one, pop and check it’s the partner. Test it on an empty string, a mismatched pair, and a string that only opens.

checkpoints.prompt: An undo history: the last change made is the first one undone. Which structure fits?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — undo is last in, first out: a stack.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the newest change comes out first: last in, first out, a stack.

checkpoints.prompt: You check thousands of times whether a student ID is registered. What should hold the IDs?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a set answers ‘is it there?’ in about one step, however many IDs it holds.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a list or a queue checks one by one. A set answers in about one step.
